title: Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations
authors_full: Maziar Raissi, Paris Perdikaris, George Em Karniadakis
affiliations: Division of Applied Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA (Raissi, Karniadakis); Department of Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA (Perdikaris)
subdomain: benchmark forward PDE solving on 1D+time cases: Burgers, nonlinear Schroedinger, Allen-Cahn (published JCP version additionally covers inverse Navier-Stokes)
industry_context: No industry or company named; academic method paper (Brown University / University of Pennsylvania), funded by DARPA EQUiPS N66001-15-2-4055, MURI/ARO W911NF-15-1-0562, AFOSR FA9550-17-1-0013.
physics_enforced_exact: General form u_t + N[u] = 0, x in domain, t in [0,T] (Eq 1), with residual f := u_t + N[u] (Eq 2). Cases: (1) Burgers: u_t + u*u_x - (0.01/pi)*u_xx = 0, x in [-1,1], t in [0,1]; u(0,x) = -sin(pi*x); u(t,-1) = u(t,1) = 0. (2) Nonlinear Schroedinger: i*h_t + 0.5*h_xx + |h|^2*h = 0, x in [-5,5], t in [0,pi/2]; h(0,x) = 2*sech(x); periodic h(t,-5) = h(t,5) and h_x(t,-5) = h_x(t,5). (3) Allen-Cahn: u_t - 0.0001*u_xx + 5u^3 - 5u = 0, x in [-1,1], t in [0,1]; u(0,x) = x^2*cos(pi*x); periodic u and u_x. Paper states the general setup encapsulates conservation laws, diffusion processes, advection-diffusion-reaction systems, and kinetic equations.
dimensionality: 1D+time (all four benchmark cases are one space dimension x plus time t)
nonlinearity: strongly nonlinear — Burgers advection u*u_x produces a sharp internal layer around t = 0.4; cubic coupling |h|^2*h in Schroedinger; quintic reaction 5u^3 - 5u in Allen-Cahn
bcs_ic_handled: Initial and boundary conditions enter only through the data loss MSE_u (= MSE_0 + MSE_b for Schroedinger) evaluated at N_u scattered initial/boundary points; periodic BCs penalized as (h(t,-5) - h(t,5))^2 + (h_x(t,-5) - h_x(t,5))^2 (Schroedinger) and analogous u, u_x terms for Allen-Cahn; discrete-time models penalize all Runge-Kutta stage values at x = -1 and x = 1 (SSE_b term).
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty — PDE residual network f is driven to zero at collocation points via an additive MSE_f term; the authors note MSE_f 'acts as a regularization mechanism that penalizes solutions that do not satisfy equation (3)'.
enforcement_details: u(t,x) is a deep neural network; a second network f(t,x) = u_t + N[u] is built by applying the chain rule through u via automatic differentiation (TensorFlow tf.gradients on the input coordinates), so the PDE operator derivatives are exact with respect to all network parameters; f is penalized at N_f collocation points. Complex-valued Schroedinger handled by a two-output real network h(t,x) = [u(t,x) v(t,x)] giving a complex-valued multi-output PINN. Discrete-time models place a multi-output network prior on [u^{n+c_1}(x), ..., u^{n+c_q}(x), u^{n+1}(x)] constrained by the implicit Runge-Kutta stage equations (Eq 9), enabling prediction over a large time-step in a single step.
network_architecture: Plain feed-forward MLPs (no modification): Burgers continuous 9 layers x 20 neurons per layer (3021 parameters); Schroedinger 5 layers x 100 neurons; discrete-time Burgers 4 layers x 50 neurons; Allen-Cahn 4 layers x 200 neurons with 101-output head (q = 100 RK stage values u^{n+c_i} plus final solution u^{n+1}).
input_representation: continuous-time models: concatenated coordinates [t, x]; discrete-time models: x only (stage values are network outputs)
output_representation: latent solution field u(t,x); Schroedinger: two real outputs forming complex h = [u v]; discrete-time: q+1 outputs = Runge-Kutta stage values u^{n+c_i} plus final-time solution u^{n+1}
loss_terms: Continuous time: MSE = MSE_u + MSE_f (Eq 4), with MSE_u = (1/N_u) sum |u(t_u^i, x_u^i) - u^i|^2 (initial+boundary data) and MSE_f = (1/N_f) sum |f(t_f^i, x_f^i)|^2 (PDE residual at collocation points). Schroedinger adds periodic-boundary term: MSE = MSE_0 + MSE_b + MSE_f (Eq 6). Discrete time: SSE = SSE_n + SSE_b (Eqs 12, 14) summing squared errors over all q+1 stage outputs at data time t^n and at Dirichlet boundaries x = -1, x = 1.
loss_weighting: fixed, unweighted plain sums of the MSE/SSE terms (no weighting scheme given)
sampling_strategy: Randomly distributed initial/boundary training points (N_u = 100 Burgers; N_0 = 50 initial + N_b = 50 boundary Schroedinger; N_n = 250 and 200 for the discrete cases) plus randomly sampled collocation points generated by space-filling Latin Hypercube Sampling (N_f = 10,000 Burgers; N_f = 20,000 Schroedinger); systematic grids over N_u in {20,...,200} and N_f in {2000,...,10000}; no adaptive refinement.
optimizer_schedule: L-BFGS (quasi-Newton, full-batch) used for all benchmarks; authors note mini-batch stochastic gradient descent and modern variants (Adam) for larger datasets; iteration counts and learning rates not stated.
training_compute: Burgers continuous-time case: model training took approximately 60 seconds on a single NVIDIA Titan X GPU card; other cases: hardware/time not stated.
uq_method: None — authors explicitly flag quantifying the uncertainty of network predictions as 'one pressing question' of future work, noting it was naturally addressed in their earlier Gaussian-process work but is not captured by the proposed methodology in its present form (Sec. 4, p. 20).
data_regime: Sparse physics-plus-boundary data with no interior observations: N_u = 100 IC/BC points (Burgers), 50 initial + 50 boundary points (Schroedinger), 250 and 200 initial-snapshot points (discrete Burgers / Allen-Cahn); high-fidelity spectral reference solutions are used only for error evaluation, not training. Collocation counts of 10,000 and 20,000 points carry the physics.
datasets_used: Burgers equation (exact analytical solution available); nonlinear Schroedinger equation (reference: Chebfun spectral Fourier discretization with 256 modes, fourth-order explicit Runge-Kutta, time-step pi/2 * 1e-6, final time pi/2); Burgers discrete-time single-step case t = 0.1 -> 0.9; Allen-Cahn equation (Chebfun, 512 Fourier modes, fourth-order explicit RK, time-step 1e-5, final time 1.0), single step t = 0.1 -> 0.9 with dt = 0.8.
baselines_compared: Prior Gaussian-process PDE solvers (Raissi et al., ref [9]; Burgers PINN error 'about two orders of magnitude lower' than the GP result; discrete-time error 'two orders of magnitude lower' than ref [9]); a standard neural network without the physics term (N_f = 0, footnote 1, p. 8); classical numerical methods (finite elements, spectral) discussed qualitatively but not benchmarked.
evaluation_metrics: relative L2-norm error between predicted and exact/spectral reference solutions (Tables 1-4, Figures 1-4)
key_quantitative_results:
- Burgers (continuous): rel. L2 = 6.7e-4 with N_u = 100 initial/boundary points and N_f = 10,000 LHS collocation points, 9x20 tanh MLP; training ~60 s on one NVIDIA Titan X GPU; about two orders of magnitude better than the Gaussian-process baseline (ref [9]).
- Burgers (discrete): implicit Runge-Kutta with q = 500 stages, single time-step dt = 0.8 from t = 0.1 to t = 0.9 with N_n = 250 data points: rel. L2 = 8.2e-4; claimed theoretical error accumulation dt^(2q) = 0.8^1000 ~ 1e-97, and 'first time that an implicit Runge-Kutta scheme of that high-order has ever been used'.
- Schroedinger: 5x100 MLP, 150 data points + 20,000 collocation points: rel. L2 = 1.97e-3 against spectral reference.
- Allen-Cahn: q = 100 stages, single step dt = 0.8, 4x200 MLP, N_n = 200: rel. L2 = 6.99e-3.
- Accuracy scales with data and collocation points (Table 1: N_u=20/N_f=2000 gives 2.9e-01, N_u=200/N_f=10000 gives 4.9e-04).
errors_reported: Burgers continuous: 6.7e-4 (headline, N_u=100, N_f=10,000); Table 1 values range from 4.9e-04 (N_u=200, N_f=10000) up to 1.2e+00 (N_u=20, N_f=7000). Table 2 (layers x neurons, N_u=100, N_f=10,000): from 7.4e-02 (2 layers x 10) to 5.6e-04 (8 x 40). Discrete Burgers: 8.2e-4 (4x50, q=500, dt=0.8); Table 3 best 9.5e-04 (3 x 50); Table 4 best 3.8e-04 (q=500, dt=0.4), worst 3.8e-01 (q=1, dt=0.8). Schroedinger: 1.97e-3. Allen-Cahn: 6.99e-3.
speedup_claims: No speedup claim versus classical solvers — authors state classical methods 'meet the robustness and computational efficiency standards required in practice' and PINNs should not be viewed as replacements; only an absolute training time (~60 s, Burgers, one NVIDIA Titan X GPU) is reported.
ablations: Four systematic studies: (T1) N_u x N_f grid for continuous Burgers (9x20 MLP) — accuracy generally improves with more IC/BC data given sufficient collocation points, though the trend is noisy/non-monotone; (T2) depth/width grid (N_u=100, N_f=10,000) — error falls from 7.4e-02 (2 layers x 10 neurons) to 5.6e-04 (8 x 40); (T3) discrete-time depth/width grid at q=500, dt=0.8 — best 9.5e-04 (3 layers x 50); (T4) Runge-Kutta stages q vs time-step dt (4x50 MLP) — q=1 (trapezoidal rule) and q=2 (4th-order Gauss-Legendre) cannot retain predictive accuracy for dt > 0.2, while q >= 32 allows very large time-steps (up to dt = 0.8 in a single step) at ~1e-04 to 1e-03 error.
stated_limitations: (1) Continuous-time models need a large number of collocation points N_f to enforce the physics constraint over the whole spatio-temporal domain; in higher dimensions the number of collocation points 'will increase exponentially' — a severe bottleneck (Sec. 2.2, pp. 11-12). (2) No theoretical guarantee that the L-BFGS-trained MSE loss converges to a global minimum; empirical success relies on well-posedness and a sufficiently expressive network (Sec. 2.1, p. 6). (3) PINNs 'should not be viewed as replacements of classical numerical methods' such as finite elements and spectral methods, which are more robust and computationally efficient (Sec. 4, p. 20). (4) No uncertainty quantification in the present form; flagged as a pressing future-work question (Sec. 4, p. 20).
failure_modes: Low-stage discrete-time models fail at large time-steps (q=1 trapezoidal and q=2 Gauss-Legendre lose accuracy beyond dt = 0.2, Table 4); a physics-free network (N_f = 0) underperforms in the small-data regime (footnote 1, p. 8); Table 1 shows non-monotone error in N_f (e.g. N_u=20 jumps to 1.2e+00 at N_f=7000), indicating optimization-landscape sensitivity; their own Gaussian-process predecessors required local linearization of nonlinear terms and lost accuracy in strongly nonlinear regimes (Sec. 1, p. 2).
reproducibility: All code and datasets publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/maziarraissi/PINNs; TensorFlow implementation with Python code snippets for u(t,x) and f(t,x) printed in the paper; architectures and point counts given but no random seeds, run statistics, or full hyperparameter configs.
quotable_finding: We must underline that, unlike any classical numerical method for solving partial differential equations, this prediction is obtained without any sort of discretization of the spatio-temporal domain. (p. 7)
relevance_rqs: RQ2: defines the canonical PINN recipe later components modify (tanh MLP, MSE = MSE_u + MSE_f, LHS collocation, L-BFGS, architecture grids); RQ3: canonical soft-penalty autodiff-residual enforcement for forward problems; RQ4: author-stated reliability caveats (no UQ, exponential collocation scaling in high dimensions, not a replacement for classical solvers). RQ1: not evidenced (no industry application).
manuscript_section: S4 methods (canonical PINN formulation and loss anatomy); T1 (forward benchmark accuracy numbers); F2 (PINN schematic/anatomy figure source)
cross_paper_links: builds-on: authors' own Gaussian-process PDE solvers (Raissi et al., arXiv:1703.10230 and arXiv:1708.00588, not in dossier) and automatic differentiation (Baydin et al.); discovery competitor: SINDy (Rudy et al. 2017, ref [15]); foundational basis for dossier items PINN-A06 (NTK analysis of this MSE = MSE_u + MSE_f loss), PINN-A07 (self-adaptive weighting of the same loss terms), PINN-B07 (XPINN domain decomposition, motivated by the high-dim collocation bottleneck stated here), PINN-B12/PINN-B13 (operator-learning successors for parametrized/high-dimensional problems). Published JCP version merges this Part I (arXiv:1711.10561) with Part II (arXiv:1711.10566, data-driven discovery).
notes_caveats: The analyzed PDF is NOT the typeset JCP article: per pdf-manifest.csv the publisher DOI download failed, and the file is the arXiv preprint arXiv:1711.10561v1 (28 Nov 2017), titled 'Physics Informed Deep Learning (Part I): Data-driven Solutions of Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations'. It contains the forward/data-driven-solution half only (continuous-time Burgers and Schroedinger; discrete-time Burgers and Allen-Cahn); the inverse-problem Navier-Stokes sections of the published JCP 2019 paper (from Part II, arXiv:1711.10566) are absent, so no inverse-problem numbers could be extracted — hence confidence=partial. All four benchmarks are 1D+time toy cases evaluated against exact/spectral references; Table 1 is single-run with a noisy, non-monotone error trend in N_f and no error bars/seeds; the ~60 s training-time claim covers only the smallest continuous Burgers case. The ~21k citation count reflects the paper's framework-founding status, not benchmark breadth.
